Protection and Quarantine (PPQ) carry out its mission to safeguard agriculture and facilitate safe trade by assuring that our response to incursions is rapid and efficient, minimizing the costs of a response. The goal of this project was to develop a web app that delivers maps and other products that communicate the potential influence of recent (1981−2025) weather changes on the seasonal activities (phenology) and establishment of 18 major invasive insects for the contiguous United States. Project deliverables will inform strategic planning by PPQ and state agencies in terms of both when and where to conduct pest surveillance. For example, a trend towards the earlier appearance of adult insects may indicate that monitoring traps should be installed earlier in the season, whereas areas that are becoming increasingly suitable for pest establishment should be prioritized for surveillance. # **Background** Recent weather trends may be promoting overwintering survival and increasing developmental rates of invasive insects, potentially allowing them to expand their range, emerge earlier, and attain higher densities over a longer growing season. The primary purpose of this project was to deliver predictions of the impacts of weather changes on the seasonal activities (phenology) and establishment risk of 18 major invasive insects that threaten agriculture in the United States to aid in early detection efforts. This project used a proven modeling system known as the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) to assess the potential impacts of recent weather trends (1981−2025) on the timing of pest activities (phenology) such as emergence, number of generations, and establishment for 18 major invasive species for the contiguous United States (CONUS; @tbl-species-list). We expected that a trend toward earlier phenological events and increasing climatic suitability would be most prevalent in the northeastern and midwestern U.S. owing to particularly large increases (3 to > 5°F) in winter and spring temperatures in these regions since 1981 (`\hyperref[ref-vose-2017]{Vose et al. 2017}`{=latex}`Vose et al. 2017`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-marvel-2023]{Marvel et al. 2023}`{=latex}`Marvel et al. 2023`{=html}). # **Goal and Objectives** Our goal was to develop a web app that delivers maps and other products that communicate the potential influence of recent (1981−2025) weather changes on the phenology and establishment of 18 major invasive insects for the contiguous United States (CONUS). The project addressed the following three objectives: 1. Evaluate trends in predictions of selected phenological events (adult emergence and egg hatch) and climatic suitability over the full 44-year period (1981–2025) and a more recent 24-year period (2001–2025). 2. Identify areas in the CONUS where trends are consistent across the 18 species, including earlier predicted pest activities, decreasing cold stress, increasing heat stress, and increasing climatic suitability. 3. Deliver and promote interactive maps in a range of user-friendly, readily accessible formats via a web app at USPest.org (), and through Extension programming and end user training. ::: {#tbl-species-list .cell tbl-cap='Invasive insect species with completed DDRP models. Raster data processing and calculations were performed using the R package *terra* v. 4.5 (`\hyperref[ref-hijmans-2025]{Hijmans 2025}`{=latex}`Hijmans 2025`{=html}). All plots were produced using the R package *ggplot2* v. 3.5.2 (`\hyperref[ref-wickham-2016]{Wickham 2016}`{=latex}`Wickham 2016`{=html}). ## **i. Overview of DDRP** The mechanics of DDRP are detailed in Barker et al. (`\hyperref[ref-barker-2020]{2020}`{=latex}`2020`{=html}). Briefly, DDRP uses a process-based modeling approach in which degree-days and climate stress are calculated daily and accumulate over time to model phenology and climatic suitability, respectively (@fig-project-diagram A). Required inputs include gridded daily minimum and maximum temperature data for a time frame of interest and a species parameter file. Models include four separate life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) plus a separately parameterized overwintering stage. Phenology models often incorporate variation in phenology using a user-defined number of time-distributed cohorts that reflect the distribution of times in which the overwintering stage completes development. DDRP uses annual accumulated climate stress units to identify two levels of temperature-based exclusion: moderate and severe. Similar to degree-days, which accumulate temperatures above a developmental threshold, climate stress units accumulate when temperatures exceed specified stress thresholds for heat or fall below thresholds for cold. The greater the accumulated stress units, the greater the potential for temperature-related exclusion. Locations not excluded by either level of stress are considered part of the potential distribution and have the highest potential for establishment based on temperature alone. Moderate stress may limit long-term establishment, although short-term establishment may still occur during favorable years. Severe stress is expected to prevent even short-term establishment, defined as survival for one complete year. Because the model considers temperature alone, it does not account for host availability or other environmental factors that may influence pest distributions. Over the daily time-step, DDRP produces outputs that include maps of the potential distribution, number of generations, life stages present, and dates of phenological events. Additionally, it integrates maps produced by the phenology and climatic suitability model to provide insight into phenology (i.e., life stage present or the date of specific event) only in areas at risk of establishment. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Workflow for producing maps for the DDRP Pest Trends web application. (A) Daily minimum and maximum temperatures (1981–2025) and species-specific model parameters served as inputs to the Degree-Days, Risk, and Phenological Event Mapping (DDRP) system. (B) DDRP models estimate pest phenology, including adult emergence and egg hatch, and climatic suitability based on cold and heat stress, which together inform potential distribution. (C) Time series analyses compare trends over the full 1981–2025 period and the more recent 2001–2025 period. (D) Individual-species outputs characterize trend direction, statistical significance, and magnitude of change. (E) Summary statistics across 18 invasive pest species identify geographic areas with consistent trends in phenology and climatic suitability.](Full_report_figs/Pest_trends_flow_diagram.png){#fig-project-diagram fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## **ii. Trend analyses for individual species** Five types of predictions produced by DDRP were retained for trend analyses for this study: (1) dates (day of year) of first adult emergence, (2) dates of first egg hatch, (3) cold stress accumulation, (4) heat stress accumulation, and (5) the potential distribution, as measured by areas not excluded by cold and heat stresses (@fig-project-diagram B). Modeling in DDRP used daily minimum and maximum temperature data for 1981 to 2025 at 4-km^2^ resolution from the PRISM (Parameter-elevation Relationships on Independent Slopes Model) (`\hyperref[ref-daly-1994]{Daly et al. 1994}`{=latex}`Daly et al. 1994`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-daly-2008]{2008}`{=latex}`2008`{=html}) database (http://www.prism.oregonstate.edu). We evaluated the direction and magnitude of changes in predictions over two periods: 1981–2025 (the full 44-year period) and 2001–2025 (the recent 25-year period; @fig-project-diagram C). Analyzing both periods allowed us to characterize long-term trends and determine whether more recent changes in predicted phenology and climatic suitability differed from patterns observed over the longer period. Trends were assessed using the Mann–Kendall test and Theil–Sen regression, two rank-based, non-parametric methods widely used for analyzing environmental and remotely sensed time series (`\hyperref[ref-goossens-berger-1986]{Goossens and Berger 1986}`{=latex}`Goossens and Berger 1986`{=html}). These methods do not require normally distributed data and are therefore suitable for environmental variables that may depart from a normal distribution. The Mann–Kendall test identifies whether an increasing or decreasing trend exists and assesses its statistical significance (`\hyperref[ref-mann-1945]{Mann 1945}`{=latex}`Mann 1945`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-kendall-1975]{Kendall 1975}`{=latex}`Kendall 1975`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-gilbert-1987]{Gilbert 1987}`{=latex}`Gilbert 1987`{=html}). Kendall’s tau quantifies the direction and strength of the trend, ranging from −1 (strong negative trend) to +1 (strong positive trend). Trends were considered statistically significant at P < 0.10, a threshold often used in spatial analyses of environmental and remotely sensed time series to identify potentially meaningful trends while accounting for variability in climatic data (`\hyperref[ref-wang-2020]{Wang et al. 2020}`{=latex}`Wang et al. 2020`{=html}). Theil–Sen regression estimates the rate of change over time as the median slope across all pairs of observations. Slopes are expressed in the relevant units per year: days per year for phenological events and cumulative climate stress units per year for cold and heat stress. For phenology, negative slopes indicate that developmental events are occurring earlier, whereas positive slopes indicate later timing. These shifts may affect seasonal activity, survival, reproduction, and establishment potential, depending on the species and its life history. Changes in annual climate stress units indicate whether temperature stress is increasing or decreasing over time. As accumulated stress units rise above predefined limits in DDRP, locations may shift from suitable to moderately or severely stress-excluded. Conversely, declining stress may allow locations to become climatically suitable as accumulated units fall below these limits. Decreasing cold stress may improve winter survival and allow range expansion into previously unsuitable areas, whereas increasing heat stress may reduce summer survival and limit establishment. The Mann-Kendall and Theil-Sen analyses were implemented in the R package `modifiedmk` v. 1.6 (`\hyperref[ref-patakamuri-2021]{Patakamuri 2021}`{=latex}`Patakamuri 2021`{=html}) and used predictions that were corrected for serial correlation (autocorrelation) using the approach of von Storch (`\hyperref[ref-von-storch-1995]{1995}`{=latex}`1995`{=html}) and Kulkarni and von Storch (`\hyperref[ref-kulkarni-von-storch-1995]{1995}`{=latex}`1995`{=html}). This correction for autocorrelation, also known as “prewhitening,” is often applied to avoid violating the Mann-Kendall test’s assumption of no autocorrelation in the time series, which may increase the likelihood of type 1 error (rejecting the null hypothesis when it might be true) (`\hyperref[ref-kulkarni-von-storch-1995]{Kulkarni and von Storch 1995}`{=latex}`Kulkarni and von Storch 1995`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-yue-2002]{Yue et al. 2002}`{=latex}`Yue et al. 2002`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-zhang-zwiers-2004]{Zhang and Zwiers 2004}`{=latex}`Zhang and Zwiers 2004`{=html}). The accumulation of degree-days and climate stresses in our models exhibits a seasonal cycle driven by temperature, which would increase autocorrelation in the time series (`\hyperref[ref-coen-2020]{Coen et al. 2020}`{=latex}`Coen et al. 2020`{=html}). A cumulative link model (CLM) was used to assess temporal changes in predicted climate suitability for establishment, represented by three ordinal categories of climate-stress exclusion: no exclusion, moderate exclusion, and severe exclusion (`\hyperref[ref-barker-2020]{Barker et al. 2020}`{=latex}`Barker et al. 2020`{=html}). The model estimates temporal trends in the probability of a location falling into each suitability category. Positive trends indicate a shift toward no exclusion, consistent with decreasing temperature-related stress and potentially more favorable conditions for establishment. Conversely, negative trends indicate a shift toward moderate or severe exclusion, consistent with increasing temperature-related stress and potentially less favorable conditions for establishment. The CLM was fitted in R using the ordinal package (v. 2023.12-4) (`\hyperref[ref-christensen-2025]{Christensen 2025}`{=latex}`Christensen 2025`{=html}), with a logit link function and the proportional odds assumption. Model coefficients (β) were used to assess the direction and magnitude of temporal trends, and corresponding P-values were used to evaluate statistical significance. Positive coefficients indicate a shift toward lower climate stress and greater potential for establishment, whereas negative coefficients indicate a shift toward greater climate stress and lower potential for establishment. Coefficients are expressed on the log-odds scale and are not restricted to a fixed range. ## **iii. Comparative analyses** Outputs from trend analyses for the 18 species (@fig-project-diagram D) were combined to identify areas where pests consistently exhibited earlier first adult emergence and first egg hatch, decreasing cold stress, and increasing heat stress (@fig-project-diagram E). Spatial descriptive statistics were calculated across species, including the mean and variance in the magnitude of change and the frequency of statistically significant increasing versus decreasing trends. Asian longhorned beetle** {#alb} :::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} ::: {style="text-align: left;"} [Download ALB report as PDF](ALB/ALB.pdf){.btn .btn-primary} ::: :::: ## **1A. Introduction** {.unlisted} The Asian longhorned beetle (ALB), *Anoplophora glabripennis* Motschulsky (Coleoptera: Cerambycidae), is a wood-eating pest native to the Korean peninsula and eastern China. In the United States, the beetle was first discovered on Long Island, NY, in 1996, where it likely arrived via wood packaging from China (`\hyperref[ref-haack-hoebeke-1996]{Haack and Hoebeke 1996}`{=latex}`Haack and Hoebeke 1996`{=html}). The pest spread to several sites in the eastern United States and Canada but has since been eradicated in Illinois, New Jersey, New York City, Boston, and Canada (`\hyperref[ref-coyle-2021]{Coyle et al. 2021}`{=latex}`Coyle et al. 2021`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-eppo-2019]{EPPO 2019}`{=latex}`EPPO 2019`{=html}). However, infestations currently persist in central Long Island, NY; Worcester County, MA; Clermont County, OH; and Charleston County, SC (`\hyperref[ref-coyle-2021]{Coyle et al. 2021}`{=latex}`Coyle et al. 2021`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-usda-aphis-2025]{USDA-APHIS 2025}`{=latex}`USDA-APHIS 2025`{=html}). ALB is a major threat to the maple hardwood lumber and sugar maple syrup industries, as well as tourism associated with fall colors in maple trees (`\hyperref[ref-smith-wu-2008]{Smith and Wu 2008}`{=latex}`Smith and Wu 2008`{=html}). The cost of a complete infestation of all urban areas in the United States has been estimated at \$669 billion (`\hyperref[ref-nowak-2001]{Nowak et al. 2001}`{=latex}`Nowak et al. 2001`{=html}). An estimated 30-35% of trees in the eastern United States are species commonly attacked by ALB (`\hyperref[ref-nowak-2001]{Nowak et al. 2001}`{=latex}`Nowak et al. 2001`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-smith-wu-2008]{Smith and Wu 2008}`{=latex}`Smith and Wu 2008`{=html}). The pest can complete its lifecycle on *Acer*, *Aesculus*, *Albizia julibrissin*, *Betula*, *Cercidiphyllum*, *Elaeagnus angustifolia*, *Fraxinus*, *Platanus*, *Populus*, *Salix*, *Sorbus aucuparia* and *Ulmus* species (`\hyperref[ref-van-der-gaag-loomans-2014]{van der Gaag and Loomans 2014}`{=latex}`van der Gaag and Loomans 2014`{=html}). However, preferred genera in North America are *Acer* and *Ulmus*, compared to *Populus* and *Salix* in China (`\hyperref[ref-hu-2009]{Hu et al. 2009}`{=latex}`Hu et al. 2009`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-van-der-gaag-loomans-2014]{van der Gaag and Loomans 2014}`{=latex}`van der Gaag and Loomans 2014`{=html}). Following oviposition under the bark of host trees, larvae feed in the cambial region before burrowing into the inner xylem and heartwood (`\hyperref[ref-haack-hoebeke-1996]{Haack and Hoebeke 1996}`{=latex}`Haack and Hoebeke 1996`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-haack-2006]{Haack 2006}`{=latex}`Haack 2006`{=html}). ALB may overwinter as an egg, larva, or pupa, though typically as an egg or larva, before emerging from round exit holes as adults (`\hyperref[ref-haack-hoebeke-1996]{Haack and Hoebeke 1996}`{=latex}`Haack and Hoebeke 1996`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-haack-2006]{Haack 2006}`{=latex}`Haack 2006`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-herard-2009]{Herard et al. 2009}`{=latex}`Herard et al. 2009`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-faccoli-2015]{Faccoli et al. 2015}`{=latex}`Faccoli et al. 2015`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-trotter-keena-2016]{Trotter and Keena 2016}`{=latex}`Trotter and Keena 2016`{=html}). Diapause termination requires a chilling period, and larvae may be freeze tolerant (`\hyperref[ref-roden-2008]{Roden et al. 2008}`{=latex}`Roden et al. 2008`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-torson-2021]{Torson et al. 2021}`{=latex}`Torson et al. 2021`{=html}). A model for ALB developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at . The full set of model parameters for ALB, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (`\hyperref[ref-coop-2018]{Coop 2018}`{=latex}`Coop 2018`{=html}). ## **1B. Results** {.unlisted} ### **i. Phenology** #### **Entire period: 1981--2025** Significant trends in predicted first adult emergence and egg hatch for ALB over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025) were predominantly negative, indicating that these phenological events shifted earlier over time (@fig-alb-emergence, @fig-alb-egg-hatch). Significant advances were concentrated across large portions of the eastern United States, with additional localized areas along the Pacific coast, in the South, and at higher elevations of the interior West. In these regions, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch decreased by approximately 0.01–0.8 days per year, with some of the largest declines occurring at higher elevations in the West. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for ALB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Discussion** {.unlisted} Predictions of phenology and climatic suitability for ALB show clear, directional changes, with the strongest and most spatially extensive signals emerging over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Predicted adult emergence and egg hatch occurred progressively earlier across large portions of CONUS, averaging 0.01–0.5 days earlier per year, which suggests that surveyors and other management staff in these areas may want to ensure that materials are prepared earlier in the season. Faster development under warmer conditions could also enable ALB to achieve more rapid population growth, increase its damage potential, and shorten or eliminate the pupal hold period, potentially increasing the likelihood of multiple generations per year (`\hyperref[ref-schmitt-2025a]{Schmitt et al. 2025a}`{=latex}`Schmitt et al. 2025a`{=html},`\hyperref[ref-schmitt-2025b]{b}`{=latex}`b`{=html}). Declines in predicted cold stress across northern and high-elevation regions—including parts of the Northeast and Midwest—may indicate increasing potential for overwinter survival in ALB. These regions may be especially vulnerable because of the high abundance of preferred host species for ALB, particularly maple (`\hyperref[ref-smith-wu-2008]{Smith and Wu 2008}`{=latex}`Smith and Wu 2008`{=html}; `\hyperref[ref-berland-elliott-2014]{Berland and Elliot 2014}`{=latex}`Berland and Elliot 2014`{=html}). Thus, surveyors and managers may want to increase the prioritization of areas such as northern New England and Michigan. Although significant increases in heat stress—and corresponding reductions in establishment risk—are predicted for the hottest parts of the Southwest, risk in this region is likely already constrained by the relatively low density of hardwood forests. The stronger and more significant trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. For example, increases in predicted cold stress in parts of the north-central United States may reflect this region's departure from the broader warming pattern during the more recent period, with some areas experiencing cooler conditions relative to the preceding years (`\hyperref[ref-ncei-2021]{NCEI 2021}`{=latex}`NCEI 2021`{=html}). \vspace{1.5em} ## **1D. Introduction** {.unlisted} The Asiatic rice borer (ASRB), *Chilo suppressalis* Walker (Lepidoptera: Crambidae), is a stem borer and major pest of rice and other grasses, including water oat, sorghum, millet, and corn, throughout Asia, Oceania, the Middle East, and Europe (`\hyperref[ref-caps-2025]{CAPS 2025}`{=latex}`CAPS 2025`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-meng-2008]{Meng et al. 2008}`{=latex}`Meng et al. 2008`{=html}). ASRB larvae cause major damage to rice crops by severing panicles or the vascular system of tillers, leading to white earheads and dead hearts (`\hyperref[ref-kiritani-iwao-1967]{Kiritani and Iwao 1967}`{=latex}`Kiritani and Iwao 1967`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-muralidharan-pasalu-2006]{Muralidharan and Pasalu 2006}`{=latex}`Muralidharan and Pasalu 2006`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-chen-2014]{Chen et al. 2014}`{=latex}`Chen et al. 2014`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-eppo-2019]{EPPO 2019}`{=latex}`EPPO 2019`{=html}). Larvae can cause substantial economic losses, with reports of 20% yield loss under some conditions (`\hyperref[ref-rahman-2004]{Rahman et al. 2004}`{=latex}`Rahman et al. 2004`{=html}). The pest is present in Hawaii and is frequently intercepted at United States ports of entry (`\hyperref[ref-solis-2006]{Solis 2006}`{=latex}`Solis 2006`{=html}). With the United States rice industry valued at over USD 6 billion in 2025 (`\hyperref[ref-childs-2025]{Childs 2025}`{=latex}`Childs 2025`{=html}), yield reductions resulting from ASRB could cause significant economic damage to rice-producing regions. A model for ASRB developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at . The full set of model parameters for ASRB, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (`\hyperref[ref-coop-barker-2020]{Coop and Barker 2020}`{=latex}`Coop and Barker 2020`{=html}). ## **2B. Discussion** {.unlisted} Although ASRB is not established in the CONUS, understanding predicted changes in phenology can inform surveillance planning. In areas with earlier phenological events, predicted dates shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.5 days per year, suggesting that surveillance materials may need to be deployed earlier in the season. The southern United States warrants particular attention because it includes major rice-producing states, such as Louisiana, Texas, and Arkansas, where surveillance could help detect potential introductions into areas with suitable host crops. Although warmer growing-season temperatures can advance ASRB emergence and increase voltinism, temperature effects on development and overwintering are context dependent. ASRB is univoltine in cooler parts of its native range, such as northern Japan, where shortening day lengths serve as the primary environmental cue for larvae to enter winter diapause. In contrast, populations in warmer regions, including Taiwan, can complete 5–6 generations annually and typically lack diapause (`\hyperref[ref-kiritani-iwao-1967]{Kiritani and Iwao 1967}`{=latex}`Kiritani and Iwao 1967`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-ramoneda-roig-1993]{Ramoneda and Roig 1993}`{=latex}`Ramoneda and Roig 1993`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-tsumuki-1994]{Tsumuki et al. 1994}`{=latex}`Tsumuki et al. 1994`{=html}). Genetic differentiation among ASRB populations in China is also associated with geographic variation in voltinism (`\hyperref[ref-meng-2008]{Meng et al. 2008}`{=latex}`Meng et al. 2008`{=html}). Warmer growing-season temperatures have been linked to earlier emergence and spring flight, increased voltinism (`\hyperref[ref-lee-2014]{Lee 2014}`{=latex}`Lee 2014`{=html}), and greater pupal weight and fecundity (`\hyperref[ref-fu-2016]{Fu et al. 2016}`{=latex}`Fu et al. 2016`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-huang-2018]{Huang et al. 2018}`{=latex}`Huang et al. 2018`{=html}). However, experimental studies found that warmer winter temperatures (10 °C versus 1 and 5 °C) reduced pupation rates, pupal weight, and post-diapause reproductive potential (`\hyperref[ref-xiao-2017]{Xiao et al. 2017}`{=latex}`Xiao et al. 2017`{=html}). Collectively, these findings suggest that the effects of temperature on ASRB development and population dynamics depend on seasonal conditions and geographic context, underscoring the importance of considering both phenological shifts and climatic suitability when prioritizing surveillance. The climate-stress maps showed regional changes in both cold and heat stress, but these changes produced little statistically significant change in predicted climatic suitability. This distinction is important because changes in individual stress variables do not necessarily translate into changes in establishment likelihood when the modeled conditions remain within the suitable range. Decreasing cold stress in portions of the northern United States and could reduce a temperature-related limitation on establishment, whereas increasing heat stress in parts of the Southwest and California could impose greater climatic constraints. However, because the climatic-suitability maps showed very few significant changes, these stress trends did not translate into widespread changes in predicted establishment likelihood. The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability. ## **2D. Introduction** {.unlisted} Native to the Mediterranean region, the honeydew moth, *Cryptoblabes gnidiella* (CGN) (Lepidoptera: Pyralidae), can act as both a primary and secondary pest of numerous economically important crops, including avocado, citrus, corn, cotton, grape, loquat, pomegranate, rice, and wheat throughout Asia, Oceania, the Middle East, and Europe (`\hyperref[ref-silva-mexia-1999]{Silva and Mexia 1999}`{=latex}`Silva and Mexia 1999`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-molet-2013]{Molet 2013}`{=latex}`Molet 2013`{=html}). It is commonly associated with coccoids and pseudococcids, which produce honeydew that serves as a food source for its larvae, although it can also directly damage the fruit of certain host plants (`\hyperref[ref-avidov-gothilf-1960]{Avidov and Gothilf 1960}`{=latex}`Avidov and Gothilf 1960`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-yehuda-1991]{Yehuda et al. 1991}`{=latex}`Yehuda et al. 1991`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-silva-mexia-1999]{Silva and Mexia 1999}`{=latex}`Silva and Mexia 1999`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-molet-2013]{Molet 2013}`{=latex}`Molet 2013`{=html}). The species has spread widely across southern Europe, parts of Africa, and several regions worldwide, including Brazil, Fiji, India, Malaysia, New Zealand, Uruguay, and Hawaii in the United States (`\hyperref[ref-eppo-2025]{EPPO 2025}`{=latex}`EPPO 2025`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-molet-2013]{Molet 2013}`{=latex}`Molet 2013`{=html}). Although it has not become established in the contiguous United States (CONUS), it is frequently intercepted at ports of entry, often originating from countries where its establishment has not been documented (`\hyperref[ref-molet-2013]{Molet 2013}`{=latex}`Molet 2013`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-velez-gavilan-2023]{Velez-Gavilan 2023}`{=latex}`Velez-Gavilan 2023`{=html}). A model for CGN developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the CONUS at . The full set of model parameters for CGN, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (`\hyperref[ref-barker-coop-2019]{Barker and Coop 2019}`{=latex}`Barker and Coop 2019`{=html}). ## **3B. Statistically significant trends were more spatially restricted, occurring primarily in portions of the southern and eastern United States and in scattered areas of the West. Within these regions, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.8 days per year, with some of the largest shifts occurring at higher elevations in the West. Discussion** {.unlisted} Although CGN is not established in the CONUS, understanding predicted changes in phenology can inform surveillance planning. In areas exhibiting significant trends toward earlier phenology, predicted dates shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.8 days per year, suggesting that surveillance materials may need to be deployed earlier in the season. Surveillance efforts may be particularly important where these trends overlap with major host-fruit production areas, including those supporting intensive cultivation of grapes, citrus, pomegranates, and avocados. Such areas include parts of the West and South, particularly California and Texas, as well as portions of the Gulf Coast. Earlier adult emergence and egg hatch could potentially allow CGN to complete more generations per year, increasing pest pressure and associated crop damage. CGN lacks a true winter diapause and can complete multiple generations under warm conditions (`\hyperref[ref-avidov-gothilf-1960]{Avidov and Gothilf 1960}`{=latex}`Avidov and Gothilf 1960`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-molet-2013]{Molet 2013}`{=latex}`Molet 2013`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-lucchi-2019]{Lucchi et al. 2019}`{=latex}`Lucchi et al. 2019`{=html}). The number of generations completed annually therefore depends partly on whether local environmental conditions permit continued development throughout the growing season. CGN can complete as many as nine generations annually in the warmest parts of its range, such as northeastern Brazil (`\hyperref[ref-ringenberg-2005]{Ringenberg et al. 2005}`{=latex}`Ringenberg et al. 2005`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-ioriatti-2012]{Ioriatti et al. 2012}`{=latex}`Ioriatti et al. 2012`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-molet-2013]{Molet 2013}`{=latex}`Molet 2013`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-ozturk-2018]{Öztürk 2018}`{=latex}`Öztürk 2018`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-lucchi-2019]{Lucchi et al. 2019}`{=latex}`Lucchi et al. 2019`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-corbetta-2025]{Corbetta et al. 2025}`{=latex}`Corbetta et al. 2025`{=html}). DDRP predictions indicate that CGN may complete at least one generation annually and up to eight generations in the South within climatically suitable areas (`\hyperref[ref-barker-coop-2019]{Barker and Coop 2019}`{=latex}`Barker and Coop 2019`{=html}). These findings underscore the importance of interpreting regional trends in predicted phenology alongside climatic suitability and the potential for multiple generations, which together determine the timing and duration of seasonal CGN activity. The climate-stress trend maps showed broad changes in both cold and heat stress, but these changes translated into statistically significant shifts in predicted climatic suitability for ECW in only a few isolated areas of California and the Southwest. The contrast between widespread climate-stress trends and limited suitability changes suggests that the modeled climatic limits remain sufficiently broad that changes in individual stress variables do not necessarily alter establishment potential. Previous modeling studies for CGN identified suitable environments for the pest throughout the South and Midwest, as well as along the West Coast, whereas cold temperatures would likely exclude the pest from colder regions, including the Intermountain West and latitudes north of *ca.* 41° N in the East (`\hyperref[ref-barker-coop-2019]{Barker and Coop 2019}`{=latex}`Barker and Coop 2019`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-zumbado-2023]{Zumbado-Ulate et al. 2023}`{=latex}`Zumbado-Ulate et al. 2023`{=html}). The results of this study suggest that these areas have remained suitable for CGN establishment over the study periods. However, a recent modeling study predicted increasing climatic suitability for CGN in the Mediterranean region, with suitable conditions shifting northward along the region’s northern margins. These findings highlight the need for further investigation into potential shifts in CGN establishment risk across the CONUS (`\hyperref[ref-rossi-2026]{Rossi et al. 2026}`{=latex}`Rossi et al. 2026`{=html}). The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability. ## **3D. Emerald ash borer** {#eab} :::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} ::: {style="text-align: left;"} [Download EAB report as PDF](EAB/EAB.pdf){.btn .btn-primary} ::: :::: ## **4A. Introduction** {.unlisted} The emerald ash borer (EAB), *Agrilus planipennis* Fairmaire (Coleoptera: Buprestidae), is a flat-headed, wood-boring beetle native to eastern Asia that relies almost exclusively on ash trees (*Fraxinus* species) to complete its life cycle (`\hyperref[ref-poland-2015]{Poland et al. 2015}`{=latex}`Poland et al. 2015`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-usda-aphis-2025]{USDA-APHIS 2025}`{=latex}`USDA-APHIS 2025`{=html}). It was first detected in North America in 2002 in Michigan and Ontario, although it likely arrived in Michigan during the early to mid-1990s (`\hyperref[ref-siegert-2014]{Siegert et al. 2014}`{=latex}`Siegert et al. 2014`{=html}). EAB is now present in 37 U.S. states and six Canadian provinces (`\hyperref[ref-eppo-2025]{EPPO 2025}`{=latex}`EPPO 2025`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-usda-aphis-2025]{USDA-APHIS 2025}`{=latex}`USDA-APHIS 2025`{=html}). Adult beetles lay eggs in bark crevices, and upon hatching, larvae burrow into the tree to feed on the inner phloem, outer xylem, and cambium. They overwinter as larvae or pre-pupae within characteristic serpentine galleries beneath the bark (`\hyperref[ref-tluczek-2011]{Tluczek et al. 2011}`{=latex}`Tluczek et al. 2011`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-poland-2015]{Poland et al. 2015}`{=latex}`Poland et al. 2015`{=html}). This feeding disrupts the tree’s ability to transport water and nutrients, typically leading to tree death within several years (`\hyperref[ref-knight-2013]{Knight et al. 2013}`{=latex}`Knight et al. 2013`{=html}). EAB’s cryptic nature, in which all life stages except for the adult beetle are inside of trees, makes early detection of this pest extremely difficult (`\hyperref[ref-haack-2002]{Haack et al. 2002}`{=latex}`Haack et al. 2002`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-usda-aphis-2025]{USDA-APHIS 2025}`{=latex}`USDA-APHIS 2025`{=html}). Previous modeling studies indicated broad climatic suitability for EAB across North America that overlapped with the ranges of native *Fraxinus* species (`\hyperref[ref-desantis-2013]{DeSantis et al. 2013}`{=latex}`DeSantis et al. 2013`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-sobek-swant-2012]{Sobek-Swant et al. 2012}`{=latex}`Sobek-Swant et al. 2012`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-liang-fei-2014]{Liang \& Fei 2014}`{=latex}`Liang & Fei 2014`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-cuddington-2018]{Cuddington et al. (2018)}`{=latex}, `\hyperref[ref-barker-2023]{Barker et al. 2023}`{=latex}`Barker et al. 2023`{=html}). All North American ash species are vulnerable to EAB, though blue ash (*F. quadrangulata* Michaux) appears to be less preferred (`\hyperref[ref-poland-2015]{Poland et al. 2015}`{=latex}`Poland et al. 2015`{=html}). In its native range, the beetle primarily infests stressed or weakened trees, whereas in North America it readily attacks both healthy and stressed individuals, with stressed trees often supporting higher beetle densities (`\hyperref[ref-poland-mccullough-2006]{Poland and McCullough 2006}`{=latex}`Poland and McCullough 2006`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-tluczek-2011]{Tluczek et al. 2011}`{=latex}`Tluczek et al. 2011`{=html}). Other members of the olive family, such as white fringetree (*Chionanthus virginicus* L.) and olive (*Olea europaea* L.), may also serve as hosts, though survival rates on these species appear to be lower (`\hyperref[ref-rutledge-arango-velez-2017]{Rutledge and Arango-Velez 2017}`{=latex}`Rutledge and Arango-Velez 2017`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-peterson-cipollini-2020]{Peterson and Cipollini 2020}`{=latex}`Peterson and Cipollini 2020`{=html}). The economic impact of EAB in the United States has reached billions of dollars, and the widespread loss of ash trees has led to reduced biodiversity and the degradation of important ecosystem services (`\hyperref[ref-kovacs-2010]{Kovacs et al. 2010}`{=latex}`Kovacs et al. 2010`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-aukema-2011]{Aukema et al. 2011}`{=latex}`Aukema et al. 2011`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-schrader-2021]{Schrader et al. 2021}`{=latex}`Schrader et al. 2021`{=html}). A model for EAB developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at . Discussion** {.unlisted} Predicted EAB phenology generally shifted toward earlier seasonal events, with the strongest and most spatially extensive trends occurring over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Predicted adult emergence and egg hatch occurred progressively earlier across portions of the East during both study periods, at rates of approximately 0.01–0.9 days per year. Because EAB is widely established across much of this region, these shifts have practical implications for monitoring and management. Pest managers may need to adjust the timing of seasonal activities to maintain their effectiveness. For example, traps targeting adult beetles may need to be deployed earlier in spring to improve early detection of new infestations, while release schedules for biological control agents, including the larval parasitoids *Spathius agrili* and *S. galinae*, may need to be adjusted to account for changes in host availability. In contrast, significant trends toward later adult emergence and egg hatch occurred in parts of the Intermountain West during 2001–2025. These localized patterns may reflect regional differences in temperature trends and seasonal warming, which have not been spatially or seasonally uniform across the United States (`\hyperref[ref-ncei-2021]{NCEI 2021}`{=latex}`NCEI 2021`{=html}). However, further analysis of temperature trends during the study period is needed to determine whether these differences explain the predicted delays. Trends in EAB's phenology should be interpreted in light of some current limitations of the phenology model. First, the model predicts adult emergence solely from degree-day accumulation and does not account for the chilling requirements of overwintering J-larvae, which must receive sufficient winter chilling to terminate obligatory diapause before metamorphosis can begin (`\hyperref[ref-duan-2021]{Duan et al. 2021}`{=latex}`Duan et al. 2021`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-duan-2026]{Duan et al. 2026}`{=latex}`Duan et al. 2026`{=html}). Because warmer chilling temperatures may delay adult emergence (`\hyperref[ref-duan-2026]{Duan et al. 2026}`{=latex}`Duan et al. 2026`{=html}), the model may overestimate advances in emergence in warmer regions of the United States, including the South. Second, the model assumes a univoltine life cycle, whereas EAB can exhibit a semivoltine life cycle in cooler regions, overwintering as early instars and requiring a second summer of feeding before reaching the J-larval stage (`\hyperref[ref-jones-2019]{Jones et al. 2019}`{=latex}`Jones et al. 2019`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-bohannon-2022]{Bohannon et al. 2022}`{=latex}`Bohannon et al. 2022`{=html}). This extended development may alter the timing and distribution of adult emergence relative to model predictions. Incorporating chilling requirements and regional variation in voltinism could therefore improve the accuracy of predicted phenological trends and their application to monitoring and biological control. The limited changes in predicted climatic suitability across both time periods indicate that trends in cold and heat stress have not produced broad changes in predicted EAB establishment potential across the CONUS. Although decreasing cold stress across portions of the Upper Midwest could potentially enhance overwintering survival in EAB, it did not substantially increase predicted establishment potential in these regions. Conversely, increasing heat stress in the Southwest may constrain establishment in already warm regions, particularly where it overlaps with the ranges of native *Fraxinus* species. The lack of substantial increases in predicted suitability in the Upper Midwest is consistent with previous findings that only sufficiently extreme cold, such as that experienced in parts of northern Canada, is likely to limit EAB establishment through overwintering mortality (`\hyperref[ref-venette-2014]{Venette et al. 2014}`{=latex}`Venette et al. 2014`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-barker-2023]{Barker et al. 2023}`{=latex}`Barker et al. 2023`{=html}). From a management perspective, these findings support continuing EAB surveillance across the CONUS rather than substantially narrowing surveillance efforts based on the observed trends in climatic suitability. Our findings were broadly consistent with Barker et al. (`\hyperlink{ref-barker-2023}{2023}`{=latex}`2023`{=html}), who reported geographically restricted trends toward earlier predicted first adult emergence of EAB over 2002–2021, including in parts of the Southeast, New England, and Upper Midwest. Our analysis also identified significant trends toward later adult emergence in parts of the interior West over 2001–2025. Both studies identified isolated areas of decreasing climatic suitability in the southwestern United States, consistent with increasing heat stress. Differences between the studies may partly reflect methodological differences, particularly our use of pre-whitening to account for temporal autocorrelation in the Mann–Kendall analysis. Pre-whitening reduces temporal autocorrelation to better satisfy the test's assumption of independence among observations and can affect the magnitude and spatial extent of statistically significant trends (`\hyperref[ref-kulkarni-storch-1995]{Kulkarni and von Storch 1995}`{=latex}`Kulkarni and von Storch 1995`{=html}). The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability. ## **4D. Introduction** {.unlisted} The Egyptian cottonworm (ECW), *Spodoptera littoralis* Boisduval (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae), is a highly destructive and polyphagous moth distributed across southern Europe, the Mediterranean Basin, the Middle East, Africa, China, and India (`\hyperref[ref-eppo-2025]{EPPO 2025}`{=latex}`EPPO 2025`{=html}). Although ECW is not established in the United States, it has been intercepted multiple times at United States ports of entry (`\hyperref[ref-ellis-2004]{Ellis 2004}`{=latex}`Ellis 2004`{=html}). Discussion** {.unlisted} Although ECW is not established in the CONUS, understanding predicted changes in phenology can inform surveillance planning. In areas exhibiting significant trends toward earlier phenology, predicted dates shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.6 days per year, suggesting that surveillance materials may need to be deployed earlier in the season. Surveillance may be particularly important where these trends overlap with major host production areas, including extensive commercial cotton acreage and intensive fruit and vegetable production across the South and along the West Coast (`\hyperref[ref-sullivan-2014]{Sullivan 2014}`{=latex}`Sullivan 2014`{=html}. However, considering trends in more northern areas is also important because migratory moths may be capable of periodic spread into northern regions later in the season (`\hyperref[ref-efsa-2015]{EFSA PLH 2015}`{=latex}`EFSA PLH`{=html}). Earlier adult emergence and egg hatch could potentially allow ECW to complete more generations per year, increasing pest pressure and associated crop damage. ECW lacks a true winter diapause and can complete multiple generations under warm conditions (`\hyperref[ref-yathom-1971]{Yathom 1971}`{=latex}`Yathom 1971`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-ellis-2004]{Ellis 2004}`{=latex}`Ellis 2004`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-miller-1977]{Miller 1977}`{=latex}`Miller 1977`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-barker-coop-2021]{Barker and Coop 2021}`{=latex}`Barker and Coop 2021`{=html}). ECW may complete 3–9 generations depending on climate and host plant (`\hyperref[ref-ellis-2004]{Ellis 2004}`{=latex}`Ellis 2004`{=html}), with 1–11 generations predicted in environmentally suitable areas in the CONUS (`\hyperref[ref-barker-coop-2021]{Barker and Coop 2021}`{=latex}`Barker and Coop 2021`{=html}). Photoperiod may also influence ECW’s response to temperature across different latitudes (`\hyperref[ref-hegazi-2021]{Hegazi et al. 2021}`{=latex}`Hegazi et al. 2021`{=html}). A laboratory study revealed interactive effects of temperature and photoperiod on ECW development, with longer photoperiods slowing larval development rates and reducing the number of larval instars (`\hyperref[ref-hegazi-2021]{Hegazi et al. 2021}`{=latex}`Hegazi et al. 2021`{=html}). Its development rate may also vary across host plant species (`\hyperref[ref-salama-1971]{Salama et al. 1971}`{=latex}`Salama et al. 1971`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-shoman-2025]{Shoman et al. 2025}`{=latex}`Shoman et al. 2025`{=html}). Higher temperatures could increase ECW reproductive rates and affect insecticide effectiveness (`\hyperref[ref-massot-2021]{Massot et al. 2021}`{=latex}`Massot et al. 2021`{=html}). The climate-stress trend maps showed broad changes in both cold and heat stress, but these changes did not translate into statistically significant shifts in predicted climatic suitability for ECW in only a few isolated areas of California (Death Valley). The contrast between widespread climate-stress trends and limited suitability changes suggests that the modeled climatic limits remain sufficiently broad that changes in individual stress variables do not necessarily alter establishment potential. Previous modeling studies reported suitable environments for ECW throughout the South and Midwest, as well as along the West Coast, whereas cold temperatures would likely exclude the pest from colder regions, including the Intermountain West and latitudes north of *ca.* 41° N in the East (`\hyperref[ref-barker-coop-2021]{Barker and Coop 2021}`{=latex}`Barker and Coop 2021`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-elshahed-2023]{ElShahed et al. 2023}`{=latex}`ElShahed et al. 2023`{=html}). The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability. ## **5D. Introduction** {.unlisted} Native to Japan, the Japanese beetle (JPB), *Popillia japonica* Newman (Coleoptera: Scarabaeidae), is a highly polyphagous pest with a host range exceeding 400 plant species, including food crops, fruit trees, turfgrass, and ornamental plant (`\hyperref[ref-fleming-1972]{Fleming 1972}`{=latex}`Fleming 1972`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-eppo-2025]{EPPO 2025}`{=latex}`EPPO 2025`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-tayeh-2023]{Tayeh et al. 2023}`{=latex}`Tayeh et al. 2023`{=html}). Since its initial detection in the United States in 1916 in New Jersey, JPB has spread widely across the eastern and central regions of the country, as well as parts of eastern Canada (`\hyperref[ref-dickerson-1918]{Dickerson and Weiss 1918}`{=latex}`Dickerson and Weiss 1918`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-fleming-1972]{Fleming 1972}`{=latex}`Fleming 1972`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-eppo-2025]{EPPO 2025}`{=latex}`EPPO 2025`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-althoff-rice-2022]{Althoff and Rice 2022}`{=latex}`Althoff and Rice 2022`{=html}). Although isolated infestations have been successfully eradicated in several western states, including Nevada and California, the beetle persists in localized areas of the Pacific Northwest, including parts of Colorado, British Columbia, Washington, and Oregon (`\hyperref[ref-althoff-rice-2022]{Althoff and Rice 2022}`{=latex}`Althoff and Rice 2022`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-eppo-2025]{EPPO 2025}`{=latex}`EPPO 2025`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-stoven-2021]{Stoven et al. 2021}`{=latex}`Stoven et al. 2021`{=html}). Total associated costs of JPB in the United States are estimated at $460 million annually, with $234 million a year spent on control and turf replacement costs (`\hyperref[ref-fleming-1972]{Fleming 1972}`{=latex}`Fleming 1972`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-usda-aphis-2015]{USDA-APHIS 2015}`{=latex}`USDA-APHIS 2015`{=html}). A model for JPB developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at . The full set of model parameters for JPB, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (`\hyperref[ref-barker-coop-2024]{Barker and Coop 2024}`{=latex}`Barker and Coop 2024`{=html}). ## **7B. Discussion** {.unlisted} Because JPB is widely established across much of the East and Midwest, trends toward earlier predicted adult emergence and egg hatch could have practical implications for monitoring and management. Pest managers may need to adjust the timing of seasonal activities to maintain their effectiveness. For example, traps targeting adult beetles may need to be deployed earlier to improve early detection of new infestations, while insecticide treatments targeting larvae may need to be applied earlier because first- and second-instar larvae are more susceptible to insecticides than older larvae. Similarly, releases of larval parasitoids, such as *Tiphia vernalis* (Rohwer), may need to be timed to coincide with earlier larval development. A trend toward earlier phenological events could increase the likelihood of univoltinism in cooler regions. Although JPB is generally univoltine in the United States, semivoltinism has been reported in colder areas, such as New England, where larvae overwinter a second winter as second or third instars in the soil, typically beneath managed turfgrass (`\hyperref[ref-fleming-1972]{Fleming 1972}`{=latex}`Fleming 1972`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-vittum-1986]{Vittum 1986}`{=latex}`Vittum 1986`{=html}). Consistent with field observations, a CLIMEX model predicted univoltinism across most of the beetle’s current North American range, but semivoltinism in the Northeast and along the United States–Canada border (`\hyperref[ref-kistner-thomas-2019]{Kistner-Thomas 2019}`{=latex}`Kistner-Thomas 2019`{=html}). Although cold stress declined for JPB in northern and high-elevation regions of the CONUS, these changes did not translate into significant shifts in predicted establishment risk. However, previous research linked JPB occurrence at its expanding range edge in the Midwest and Great Plains to minimum temperatures and long-term weather trends (`\hyperref[ref-kucherov-2025]{Kucherov et al. 2025}`{=latex}`Kucherov et al. 2025`{=html}), suggesting that changes in cold stress could influence its distribution over time. Declining cold stress may also reduce the effectiveness of *Ovavesicula popilliae*, a microsporidian biocontrol agent that increases JPB larval mortality under cold overwintering conditions (`\hyperref[ref-smitley-2026]{Smitley et al. 2026}`{=latex}`Smitley et al. 2026`{=html}). In contrast, Kucherov *et al.* (`\hyperlink{ref-kucherov-2025}{2025}`{=latex}`2025`{=html}) found negative associations between JPB occurrence and maximum temperature, consistent with our finding of significant declines in predicted climatic suitability across the Southwest and California, where heat stress increased over both the entire (1981–2025) and recent (2001–2025) periods. These declines also align with evidence that JPB survival is low under hot, dry conditions ( `\hyperref[ref-fleming-1972]{Fleming 1972}`{=latex}`Fleming 1972`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-vittum-1986]{Vittum 1986}`{=latex}`Vittum 1986`{=html}, `\hyperref[ref-allsopp-1996]{Allsopp 1996}`{=latex}`Allsopp 1996`{=html}). The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability. ## **7D.
